summary: On deep space missions, isolation, confinement, and distance from Earth create serious mental health challenges for astronauts, especially when communication delays with doctors can reach 24 minutes. To address this, we developed OverView, a low-cost, all-in-one health and behavior monitoring system that pairs a custom physical device with an easy-to-use desktop app to minimize the need for a live health advisor. On the hardware side, we built a three-channel non-hair-bearing EEG and ECG device using an ESP32 and AD8232, applying Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) and Welch's method to obtain clean brainwave signals. On the software side, we used OpenCV for facial mimic and blinking analysis, and scikit-image to combine astronauts' written journals with kinematic data and NASA's existing parameters. Built with Flutter for cross-platform desktop use, our interface calculates a fatigue score through our fatigue index algorithm, lets astronauts track their health status in one place, and provides practical mental healthcare advice. Beyond spaceflight, this solution has the potential to accelerate health monitoring processes and lower healthcare costs worldwide.
details:
What It Does and How It Works

OverView. is an all-in-one hardware and software solution designed to autonomously monitor astronauts' cognitive fatigue and mental well-being during space missions. The system operates in three core stages:

​1. Multi-Modal Data Collection: The platform gathers existing parameters from NASA databases—including motor skills tests and written astronaut mission journals—alongside real-time behavioral data from facial mimic/blinking analysis and physiological signals from our wearable EEG/ECG device.

​2. Signal and Data Processing: Brain signals captured by the hardware are processed using Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) to separate brainwave frequencies, followed by Welch’s method to obtain cleaner, noise-reduced signals. Meanwhile, written astronaut journals are combined with kinematic data using scikit-image to derive meaningful mental health insights.

​3. Fatigue Scoring and Guidance: Using these parameters, our fatigue index algorithm calculates a comprehensive fatigue score. Through a cross-platform desktop interface, astronauts can monitor their health status and receive actionable advice on maintaining their mental well-being.

​Benefits and Intended Impact

​Mission Autonomy: Minimizes the need for a real-time health advisor when communication with Earth is delayed by up to 24 minutes.

​Proactive Mental Healthcare: Enables early detection of mental instability and fatigue caused by long-term isolation and confinement.

​Worldwide Impact: Designed to be simple, practical, and low-cost, the solution also aims to reduce healthcare costs and accelerate remote patient monitoring processes on Earth.

​Tools, Hardware, and Software Used

​Hardware: ESP32 microcontroller, AD8232 sensor module, and a custom three non-hair-bearing EEG channels and ECG device.

​Software & Frameworks: Flutter framework (enabling deployment across all desktop platforms), OpenCV (for facial mimic and blinking analysis), and scikit-image (for combining journal data with kinematic metrics).

​Signal Processing & References: Fast Fourier Transform (FFT), Welch’s method, NASA Motor Skills Test datasets, and NASA ISS human-factors UI practices.

​Creativity and Factors Considered

What makes OverView. unique is its multi-modal fusion—combining neurophysiological signals (EEG/ECG), computer-vision behavioral tracking (mimics and blinking), and historical astronaut journal/kinematic data into a single, low-cost, all-in-one system. Our team specifically addressed two of the five primary Hazards of Human Spaceflight: Isolation & Confinement and Distance from Earth (24-minute delay). To ensure practicality in spacecraft environments, we utilized non-hair-bearing EEG channels for quick, hassle-free setup and modeled the user interface after NASA's ISS usability practices so astronauts can effortlessly interpret their health metrics without external assistance.
